Tap Start sleep when the baby falls asleep and Woke up when they wake. Naps and nights are told apart by the time of day, and the next nap is learned from these.
Sleep: a nap or a night, in the crib, in arms or in the sling. Log it after the fact here if you missed the timer.
Feed: breast (pick the side), bottle with millilitres, or solids. Run it as a timer, or log it after.
Pumping: how much and when. The time is kept so day milk and night milk can be told apart; night milk carries more melatonin.
Diaper: wet, dirty or both. Handy when the paediatrician asks how many a day.
Daylight: time outdoors or by a bright window. Light in the early afternoon helps the body clock and night sleep.
Routine: the steps before a nap or bedtime, like a bath, a feed, a song. The same steps each time tell the baby sleep is coming.
Note: anything else worth remembering, such as medicine, a cold, teething or a new place.
Midnight is at the top and the day goes round clockwise. Sleep is the outer ring; feeds, pumping and daylight are inside; dots mark diapers.

Before 5–6 months many naps are a single sleep cycle, about 30–45 minutes. Short naps are common at this age and usually lengthen with age.
A nap that starts inside the wake window, a dim room, or a contact nap in arms or in the sling can help it run longer. Some days naps simply stay short.

There\'s no right length. Before 5–6 months many naps are one sleep cycle, about 30–45 minutes, and naps from 30 minutes to 2 hours are all common. The whole day\'s sleep matters more than any one nap.
There\'s no right length. From about 6 months naps often join two sleep cycles and last 1–2 hours, with fewer naps a day. The whole day\'s sleep matters more than any one nap.
A baby who wakes calm from a short nap may have had enough for now. One who wakes upset can sometimes go back to sleep with a few minutes of help, or in arms or the sling.

Waking at night is normal in the first year. The longest stretch usually grows month by month, at each baby\'s own pace.
Daylight in the afternoon, a calm routine and a bedtime close to the usual one support the night. Feeding at night is part of this age.

Keep the room dark until it\'s time to start the day, keep the first minutes quiet, and look at whether the last window before bed was much shorter or longer than usual.

A walk outside, in the sling or the pram, counts. Time by a bright window helps too. Evenings dim.
A short routine repeated each evening is linked to easier bedtimes and longer nights.
Write the steps once in Settings › Routine steps, then tick them as you go. A few calm steps are enough.
Around 3–5 months sleep changes how it\'s built: lighter phases appear, and waking between cycles can increase for a while. It\'s development, a step forward.
Keep the routine, follow the baby\'s windows, and give it a few weeks. Patterns › What changed shows how it\'s going.

If you\'d like the baby to also fall asleep other ways, now and then lay the baby down drowsy, with no rush and no pressure.
On the back, on a firm, flat surface, in the baby\'s own space in your room, with nothing else in the crib: no pillows, bumpers or loose blankets. Not on a sofa or armchair.

0 to 1 month · Newborns sleep in short pieces around the clock, day and night alike. Feeding often is part of it. Rest when you can.
1 to 2 months · Short naps and naps in arms are common now; the day\'s rhythm is still forming. If your arms get tired, a sling keeps them free.
2 to 3 months · Daylight in the afternoon and a calm, dim evening help the body clock that is forming now.

3 to 4 months · Sleep is changing how it\'s built, so some nights may have more wakings for a while. It\'s development, at the baby\'s own pace. When the baby starts trying to roll, it\'s time to stop swaddling.
4 to 6 months · Wake windows grow, and many babies settle into three or four naps. A short routine, the same each time, helps everyone know what comes next.
6 to 8 months · Play and exploring fill more of the awake time. Rolling and sitting are new skills, and practising them is part of the day.
8 to 10 months · Many babies move to two naps around now. Days with a longer awake time are normal while the change settles.
10 to 12 months · Standing and new sounds can stir the night for a few days. A familiar routine is a steady place to come back to.
12 to 15 months · Total sleep is usually 11 to 14 hours a day, naps included. Each child finds their own place in that range.
15 to 18 months · Many toddlers move to one nap, often after lunch. The change can take a few weeks of back and forth.
18 to 21 months · Wanting to choose arrives. Two small choices at bedtime (which pyjamas, which book) keep the routine calm.
21 to 24 months · One nap and a regular bedtime are common now. Daylight, movement and a calm evening still help the night.
